articles.title: Paula Badosa gana en 10 minutos y no nota los 40 días de parón
articles.standfirst: La tenista nacida en Nueva York, verdugo de Kasatkina, se motiva especialmente en la ciudad de los rascacielos
articles.summary: La tenista nacida en Nueva York, verdugo de Kasatkina, se motiva especialmente en la ciudad de los rascacielos
articles.body: Paula Badosa nació en Nueva York el 15 de noviembre de 1997. Eso la convierte en un peligro en la ciudad de los rascacielos con independencia de su momento por su motivación extra para hacerlo bien. A pesar de los 40 días sin competir, tras una intervención que le privó de participar en la gira previa de torneos por Norteamérica, la catalana certificó este miércoles su pase a la segunda ronda del US Open tras apear a Daria Kasatkina, por 6-1 y 6-4. El duelo que debió terminar el martes, y se suspendió por la lluvia tras tres bolas de clasificación, acabó 24 horas después en apenas 10 minutos. Paula empata a cuatro victorias el cara a cara entre ambas. Para encontrar su último partido oficial había que remontarse al 24 de julio en Hamburgo. Badosa y Kasatkina personifican dos realidades totalmente diferentes. La ambición de la primera contrasta con la sensación de haberse dejado ir de Dasha, que triunfó en su día como rusa y que ahora pasa sin hacer ruido por la WTA como australiana. Cada uno de sus turnos de saque era una oportunidad de rotura para su rival, tanto por el porcentaje como la escasa velocidad. La pupila de Pol Toledo, una de las tenistas que más fuerte le pega, aceptaba todos los regalos. Se anotó la manga inicial cediendo un único juego. A la novena bola de triunfo fue la vencida para ella. Paula, de 28 años y la 87 de las listas, tiene en los cuartos de 2024 su mejor resultado en el Abierto estadounidense. Se ausentó de la pasada edición por lesión. El triunfo le vale 70 puntos, que son los mismos que sumó esta campaña en el Open de Australia. No jugó en Roland Garros y perdió a la primera en Wimbledon. Badosa espera en la segunda ronda a Coco Gauff. La estadounidense, cuarta cabeza de serie, viene de adjudicarse el WTA 1000 de Cincinnati. La campeona del US Open en su edición de 2023 es una de las cuatro jugadoras que aspira a salir del torneo neoyorquino con el número uno debajo del brazo. La española se agarra a sus 17 victorias ante rivales del 'top10', la última de ellas frente a Coco en los octavos del 500 de Berlín.

articles.title: Badosa - Gauff: horario y dónde ver en TV y online la segunda ronda del US Open
articles.standfirst: La tenista catalana se ha impuesto en cinco de los ocho precedentes entre ambas
articles.summary: La tenista catalana se ha impuesto en cinco de los ocho precedentes entre ambas
articles.body: Paula Badosa, después de apear a la australiana Daria Kasatkina en la primera ronda del US Open 2026, mira al futuro con optimismo a pesar de tener que enfrentarse este viernes con Coco Gauff. La estadounidense, cuarta del ranking y campeona del torneo hace apenas tres años, viene en forma como lo demuestra su reciente título en el WTA 1000 de Cincinnati. Badosa, sin embargo, no renuncia a dar la sorpresa. Con más a ganar que a perder, tras perderse toda la gira americana de pista dura a causa de una intervención, se agarra al hecho de que Coco se le da especialmente bien. Acumula 17 victorias por 22 derrotas ante adversarias del 'top10'. De los ocho precedentes entre ambas se ha anotado cinco. El último de ellos fue en los octavos del torneo de categoría 500 de Berlín. Gauff es una de las cuatro tenistas que pueden salir de Nueva York como números uno. Las otras tres son Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina y Jessica Pegula. El partido de segunda ronda del último grande entre Badosa y Gauff se jugará este viernes 4 de septiembre en uno de los estadios del Billie Jean King Tennis Center, en un horario todavía por confirmar. El partido entre Paula Badosa y Coco Gauff de la segunda ronda del US Open se podrá ver en Movistar+. También podrás seguir la última hora y todo lo que ocurra en el encuentro a través de MARCA.com y Radio MARCA.

articles.title: Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend win second-round US Open matches in warp speed
articles.summary: Americans Jessica Pegula and Taylor Townsend are among the first US Open players into the third round after quick wins on Wednesday, Sept. 2.
articles.body:
Day 4 of US Open singles draw play generated quick wins for American tennis stars Jessica Pegula and Taylor Townsend.

This is good news because rain has been an issue for the tournament, and players are still concluding first-round matches in an effort to catch up.

In the luck of the draw, Pegula and Townsend have not dealt with rain or weather-related issues. They needed 56 and 48 minutes, respectively, to secure their wins.

Pegula lost just four games, defeating fellow American Sofia Kenin, 6-3, 6-1.

August 31, 2026; New York, United States; Taylor Townsend of the U.S. in action during her first round match against Poland's Maja Chwalinska. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images

Townsend lost two games, and in an amazing stat, won every one of her first serve points (23-for-23) in her 6-1, 6-1 win over Australian Taylah Preston.

Besides advancing in singles, Townsend, 30, will play women's doubles with longtime partner Katerina Siniakova. The duo is the top-seeded team in a US Open draw that also includes Venus and Serena Williams.

The US Open is the only Grand Slam Townsend has never won in doubles. She won Wimbledon in 2024, the Australian Open in 2025 and the 2026 French Open, all with Siniakova.

It's early in the tournament, and there is a lot of tennis to be played, but Pegula and Townsend are proving they are names to watch as the US Open moves into the latter rounds.

Watch the US Open on ESPN through Sept. 13.

articles.title: “Distracting The Actual Player”: Influencers Called Out For US Open Behavior By Sports Broadcaster
articles.summary: With the game locked at deuce in the second set of the fourth game of her first-round match at the 2026 US Open, Naomi Osaka had to hold her serve upon an in...
articles.body:
With the game locked at deuce in the second set of the fourth game of her first-round match at the 2026 US Open, Naomi Osaka had to hold her serve upon an instruction from the umpire. You would think that having to stop the action at such a crucial stage of the game was because of an injury or a controversial call. But that was not the case. The umpire had to put the game on hold to address some attendees who appeared to be influencers and had begun staging a proper photoshoot session in a way that seemed to be distracting the players.

As expected, the incident has gone on to spark plenty of backlash and criticism from tennis fans. Influencer and sports broadcaster Emily Austin also weighed in on the situation, sharing her frustration over such behavior on X .

"I'm technically an 'influencer' too," she wrote. "So maybe I'm allowed to say it: The US Open is not your personal content studio. Take the pictures. Make the TikToks. Have fun. But if your content is distracting the actual players, you've forgotten why you were invited in the first place."

The incident happened during Naomi Osaka 's opening-round game against world No. 101 Anastasia Zakharova at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Monday. While the game was going on, a group of people who appeared to be creators or influencers, sitting in a corporate hospitality suite directly behind the umpire's chair, began posing for photos. They even brought out and used bright, portable lights to properly capture whatever content they were creating, further creating a major visual distraction during active play.

And as a result, chair umpire Kader Nouni paused the match, turned toward the suite, and made an announcement over the microphone, asking them to stop and take their seats.

"Guys, please, in the suite behind me, thank you guys, please take your seat," he said.

The pause appeared to throw Osaka off her rhythm because when play resumed, her ball toss went awry, forcing her to apologize to Zakharova and reset. In fact, she ultimately lost that specific point, handing her opponent the advantage, although she eventually recovered to win the match in straight sets via two tiebreaks.

Reacting to the incident, head of US Open communications Brendan McIntyre defended the umpire's action while emphasizing that although fans and guests should be able to enjoy themselves at the tournament, their activities should not become a distraction to the players or interfere with the action on court.

"We want our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend the US Open, but we also need to ensure that it does not interfere with the action and competition on the court. These instances happen infrequently, and similar to when crowd noise reaches a certain level, our chair umpires have the ability to address the crowd when they occur," he said.

Some sections of fans are blaming the US Open's decision to invite accredited digital creators to the tournament, as the tournament reportedly approved passes for close to 100 digital creators for this year's event. This, they believe, has led to attendees who do not even care about the sport and therefore disregard strict tennis etiquette.

However, this tension with digital creators and influencers appears to be nothing new in the tennis world. In April 2025, Australian tennis player Daria Saville also expressed her frustration in a TikTok video, with her criticism focused on the corporate and marketing side of tennis, which she felt was increasingly giving more attention to major fashion and lifestyle brand deals involving influencers and tennis WAGs rather than the "actual, sweaty tennis players" who live the grind of the tour.

It is, however, quite understandable that the US Open extended invitations to digital creators in a bid to promote the tournament and make tennis more appealing, especially to a younger audience. Perhaps, in their focus on the benefits of bringing these creators closer to the action, they may not have fully considered that individuals who do not have an existing appreciation for tennis might end up struggling to understand or respect the etiquette expected during a live match.

articles.title: Group of influencers forces pause during US Open match with cringeworthy photoshoot in suite
articles.summary: A viral video shows credentialed influencers disrupting Naomi Osaka's U.S. Open match at Arthur Ashe Stadium, forcing the chair umpire to intervene.
articles.body: You could argue that the overwhelming number of influencers attending the U.S. Open are doing their job – having an influence on tennis' final Grand Slam of the year – but one could also say they're doing so in the worst, most negative way imaginable. Influencers and celebrities attending the U.S. Open simply to be seen is nothing new. After all, it's one of tennis' biggest events and is held in New York City. Posing for photos, hoping to be caught on a broadcast, or simply taking advantage of an invite for a luxury outing in a suite is one thing, but causing a pause in the action would be crossing a line. Well, in one of the most stereotypical 2026 moments imaginable, that's exactly what unfolded on Monday night at Arthur Ashe Stadium. AMERICAN TENNIS STAR AMANDA ANISIMOVA LEAVES FANS CONVINCED SHE DRANK BEER MID-MATCH WITH MYSTERY BEVERAGE As four-time Grand Slam winner Naomi Osaka was preparing to serve at deuce during the fourth game of the second set against Anastasia Zakharova, the chair umpire, Kader Nouni, took a moment to address a group that was causing a disturbance. "Guys, please, in the suite behind me, thank you guys, please take your seat," Nouni said to the audience. One video shared on TikTok that has gone viral across social media shows a woman using a large, very bright light to capture content during the middle of Osaka's match. Another video shows a large group of influencers in a suite collectively recording some sort of promotion, asking their audience, "Did you miss us?" Perhaps the most eye-opening aspect of the entire situation is that the United States Tennis Association (USTA) has brought this type of scenario upon itself at the U.S. Open. HATERS OF FASHION ATTACK ARYNA SABALENKA WITH 'STREETWALKER' INSULT SIMPLY BECAUSE SHE WORE FISHNET AT US OPEN Content creators, 54 to be exact, were credentialed as media for the first time at the 2025 U.S. Open. This year, that number of credentialed influencers is "close to 100," according to USTA director of media operations Jeanmarie Daly. "We realized we live in a world where traditional media and content creators reach different audiences in different ways," Daly told Front Office Sports ahead of this year's tournament. "Our goal for the program was to have the broadest possible spectrum of coverage for the tournament." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Osaka went on to win her opening round, every-so-slightly-delayed match against Zakharova in straight sets.

articles.title: A Munar le falla el físico ante Rinderknech y se va del US Open
articles.standfirst: El balear pagó el cansancio del maratón del domingo con Terence Atmane
articles.summary: El balear pagó el cansancio del maratón del domingo con Terence Atmane
articles.body: La habitual chispa de Jaume Munar no estuvo presente este miércoles en la segunda ronda del US Open que le enfrentó a Arthur Rinderkench. El galo, vigésimo sexto cabeza de serie del cuadro, se mostró siempre más entero físicamente que su rival para cerrar un marcador de 7-6(4), 6-2 y 7-5. Las opciones de Munar para acceder a la tercera ronda se dilapidaron tras perder una renta de 5-2 en la manga inicial. Rinderknech, sin esperarlo, se encontró con una ventaja en el tanteo que no dejó escapar. Su víctima tuvo que llamar al fisioterapeuta de la organización para tratar su muslo derecho. Jaume venía de jugar casi cinco horas y con el tobillo vendado en el debut del domingo con Terence Atmane. Ese esfuerzo, sin duda, le pasó factura. El balear se centrará ahora en llegar en las mejores condiciones físicas a la serie de Copa Davis en Santiago de Chile contra el conjunto anfitrión los días 19 y 20 de septiembre. En juego, un billete para la Final a 8 de Bolonia. Munar disputará el punto del dobles al lado de Pedro Martínez.

articles.title: In 2010, two players walked onto Wimbledon’s Court 18 and played the longest match in tennis history. It didn’t end for three days, and the electronic scoreboard broke before they did
articles.summary: International Sports News: Explore the incredible journey of John Isner and Nicolas Mahut during their historic 2010 Wimbledon match, which lasted over 11 hours and broke multiple records, captivating fans worldwide.
articles.body: A tennis match that lasted 11 hours and five minutes, stretched across three days, produced 183 games, and eventually broke the electronic scoreboard sounds more like a story written for television than something that actually happened at Wimbledon. Yet that was precisely what unfolded when American John Isner and France's Nicolas Mahut met in the first round of the 2010 Championships. Their fifth set alone lasted eight hours and 11 minutes, longer than some entire professional matches, while both players repeatedly served to stay alive in a contest that seemed to have no natural ending. By the time Isner finally won 70-68, the match had become a record that remains untouched and a sporting absurdity that later inspired an HBO mockumentary.The match that refused to endIsner and Mahut began their first-round match on Court 18 at the All England Club on June 22, 2010, and neither could have known that they were about to spend three days playing one of the most extraordinary matches in tennis history.The opening four sets were already a serious contest, with Isner taking the first 6-4 before Mahut levelled with a 6-3 set. Mahut then edged the third 7-6, only for Isner to take the fourth by the same scoreline and force a deciding set.That was where the match became something entirely different.With the final set requiring a player to win by two clear games, neither man could create the decisive break. They held serve again and again as the score climbed through the 20s, 30s and 40s, with the match already far beyond anything Wimbledon had seen before.Play had originally been suspended because of fading natural light after the first four sets on June 22. The players returned the following day, but the fifth set still could not be completed, with darkness once again forcing the match to be stopped.They came back for a third day on June 24, still locked together.By then, even the electronic scoreboard had effectively conceded defeat. It stopped functioning at 47-47 in the fifth set because it had not been programmed to record a score that high.70-68: the fifth set that became its own matchThe numbers from the deciding set are difficult to comprehend even when written down.The fifth set lasted eight hours and 11 minutes and contained 138 games, with the players producing an astonishing 215 aces across the entire match: Isner hit 112 and Mahut 103.They also held serve for 168 consecutive games during the match, while Mahut had to serve to stay alive 63 times.There were only three service breaks in the entire contest.Eventually, after hours of holding serve, Isner finally won the 137th game of the fifth set to move ahead, before breaking Mahut in the following game to end the marathon at 70-68.The complete score read 6-4, 3-6, 6-7, 7-6, 70-68, with the match lasting 665 minutes, or 11 hours and five minutes.The final set alone was longer than the longest baseball game on record, which lasted eight hours and six minutes.The 183 games played overall were also 71 more than the previous highest total at Wimbledon, while the 138 games in the fifth set were 26 more than had been played in any other match.Isner and Mahut had also eclipsed the previous record for aces in a match, which had stood at 78, with their combined total of 215."I have never seen anything like it," Isner said afterwards, while the scale of what had happened was summed up by his prediction that "Nothing like this will ever happen again, ever."Neither player was quite the same afterwardsThe physical demands of the match became obvious immediately.Isner returned to the court for his second-round match against Dutchman Thiemo de Bakker, but lost in straight sets, with the effects of the three-day battle clearly still hanging over him.Mahut's defeat was equally extraordinary in its own way. Despite losing, he had produced one of the most remarkable individual performances in tennis history, with the two players setting records for points, games and aces that were unlikely to be approached again.The appeal of the match was not simply the final score, however, because as the fifth set moved beyond 50-50, both players were visibly exhausted while continuing to produce the physical effort required to keep the contest alive. Mahut repeatedly chased balls at full stretch, while Isner was visibly struggling between points, yet neither could find the small lapse that would finally end the contest.The fact that it was a first-round match on an outside court made the spectacle even stranger, with two players who were not among the sport's biggest global stars suddenly becoming the centre of attention as word spread about what was happening on Court 18.The match was so extraordinary that Wimbledon later commemorated it with a plaque outside Court 18.Isner and Mahut met again in the first round at Wimbledon in 2011, but there was no repeat marathon, with Isner winning in straight sets.The record changed tennisThe Isner-Mahut marathon was possible because of the Grand Slam rules in place at the time, which required the final set to continue until one player established a two-game advantage.That system has since changed at the major tournaments, making another 70-68 deciding set increasingly difficult to imagine.Wimbledon now uses a tie-break when the final set reaches 12-12, while the Australian Open uses a first-to-10-point super tie-break at 6-6. The French Open has also retained the advantage-set principle in its deciding sets.Isner himself would later find himself at the centre of another Wimbledon marathon. In the 2018 semi-finals, he lost to South Africa's Kevin Anderson 7-6, 6-7, 7-6, 4-6, 24-26 after six hours and 36 minutes.That match became the fourth-longest in tennis history and the second-longest at a Grand Slam, but the repeated marathon matches contributed to Wimbledon eventually introducing its fifth-set tie-break.Other records remain well behind Isner and Mahut's mark. The longest Grand Slam final in the Open Era was the 2012 Australian Open final, where Novak Djokovic defeated Rafael Nadal 5-7, 6-4, 6-2, 6-7, 7-5 after five hours and 53 minutes.The longest women's singles match lasted six hours and 31 minutes, with Vicki Nelson beating Jean Hepner 6-4, 7-6 at the 1984 Central Fidelity Banks International tournament.The longest doubles match came at the 2013 Davis Cup, when Tomas Berdych and Lukas Rosol defeated Switzerland's Stanislas Wawrinka and Marco Chiudinelli 6-4, 5-7, 6-4, 6-7, 24-22 after seven hours and two minutes.None came close to the 11-hour, three-day ordeal in south-west London.From Wimbledon absurdity to HBOThe story eventually travelled well beyond tennis.The 2010 marathon helped inspire HBO's "7 Days in Hell", a mockumentary starring Andy Samberg and Kit Harington about two fictional tennis players locked in an impossibly long Grand Slam match.Samberg later recalled watching the real-life Isner-Mahut match with writer Murray Miller and joking that somebody should make a film about a tennis match that simply never ends.That joke became the 2015 HBO film, which exaggerated the premise to comic extremes, but its starting point was very real: two players, three days, 11 hours and five minutes, 183 games and a fifth set that reached 70-68 before anyone could finally walk off Court 18.More than 16 years later, the Isner-Mahut match remains the Guinness World Record holder for the longest professional tennis match ever played.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body:
Rain has become a defining feature of this year's US Open, causing match delays for the second consecutive day.

Ben Shelton defeated Hubert Hurkacz in a four-set thriller to advance to the third round.

In the women's draw, top-ranked American Jessica Pegula defeated Sofia Kenin in straight sets.

Below, you'll find analysis of the top matches, tomorrow's schedule, and more.

No. 7 Daniil Medvedev def. Sebastian Gorzny, 6-1, 6-3, 7-5

Ben Shelton delivered an epic performance at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Wednesday, defeating Hubert Hurkacz in four sets to move on to the third round.

The 23-year-old dictated most of the match from his first serve, winning 73 percent of points.

Although Hurkacz won the second set and kept the match competitive with his powerful serve, Shelton's return game and physicality ultimately made the difference.

The 23-year-old won 45 percent of return points on Hurkacz's second serve while hitting 44 winners.

The second round of the US Open will begin Thursday on ESPN, with all matches also being available on ESPN Unlimited.

Match times have not yet been determined.

The top-ranked American continued to dominate on her serve, winning 83 percent of points while committing just 8 unforced errors.

articles.title: Jódar frena ante Bu y se despide en su estreno neoyorquino
articles.standfirst: El madrileño, siempre por detrás, cede en tres rápidos sets y se aleja del 'top10' y las ATP Finals de Turín
articles.summary: El madrileño, siempre por detrás, cede en tres rápidos sets y se aleja del 'top10' y las ATP Finals de Turín
articles.body: Rafa Jódar llegaba con toda la ilusión del mundo a su primer US Open entre los profesionales. Había ganado dos años antes entre los júniors. Es casi todo nuevo para él en sus primeros ocho meses en el circuito, pero su regularidad le permitía soñar con las ATP Finals de Turín y optar ya a ingresar en el 'top10' mundial. Nadie ha sumado más triunfos que él esta campaña, con un total de 49. Jódar tuvo ese mal día en la oficina en el peor momento, el que debutaba en el grande neoyorquino. Su verdugo fue Yunchaokete Bu, por 6-2, 6-1 y 6-1. La organización programó el partido en la pista 17, más conocida por estar pegada al Corona Park y atraer el humo de la marihuana que tanto molesta a los tenistas. La más de hora de parón por la lluvia, con 4-1 en el tercer set para Bu, tampoco ayudó a la reacción del decimosegundo cabeza de serie del cuadro. Con un 52 por ciento de primeros saques y 37 errores no forzados se hacía difícil pensar en darle la vuelta ante un Yunchaokete iluminado. Hasta siete veces le robó el saque a su oponente. Jódar pareció cansado desde el primer punto, empapado y afectado por el 70 por ciento de humedad de la ciudad de Nueva York. Su lenguaje corporal no era el mejor (se agachaba) y el 'lucky loser' chino se dio cuenta de ello muy rápido. Afincado en España y tutelado por Ricardo Ojeda, sabía lo que tenía que hacer en cada momento. Rafa mandaba a encordar una raqueta tras otra buscando una solución. Bu, que ni se inmuta, se mostraba intocable al servicio contra un adversario que es el cuarto mejor restador del circuito. El madrileño no se despedía en la primera ronda de un torneo desde el Masters 1000 de Indian Wells, a principios de marzo, cuando cedió con el chileno Alejandro Tabilo. Volverán a verse las caras el 19 y 20 de septiembre en la serie de Copa Davis en Santiago de Chile, con un billete en juego para la Final a 8 de Bolonia. Un aprendizaje más para Rafa, que volverá más fuerte y más hecho.

articles.title: Ben Shelton avoids U.S. Open upset scare from unseeded Hubert Hurkacz in close four-set victory
articles.summary: Shelton moves on to the third round at the U.S. Open for the fourth time in his career.
articles.body:
Wednesday's slate of men's singles matches was highlighted by the top-seeded American Ben Shelton taking on the unseeded Hubert Hurkacz from Poland.

Shelton - seeded 8th overall in the men's draw - has now had back-to-back four-set matchups in the 2026 U.S. Open.

The American bested Hurkacz on Wednesday, 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (7-3), and 7-5. Shelton was overcome with emotion after the close match and had quite the celebration after clinching the final point.

The 2026 U.S. Open hasn't been the smoothest sailing to the start of a major for the American star. Shelton dropped the first set of his first-round matchup against Tallon Griekspoor, but was able to bounce back with three straight sets to take the match.

After Wednesday's victory, Shelton is through to the third round and will face the winner of Denis Shavlov and Luca Van Assche, both unseeded, who play later on Wednesday.

This is the sixth U.S. Open of the 23-year-old's career. His best finish so far came in 2023, when he made it all the way to the semifinals. Shelton faced No. 2 Novak Djokovic, but lost in straight sets, 3-6, 2-6, 6-7 (4-7).

The third round has been a tough one for Shelton at this Grand Slam. He has reached the round three times before this year, and has lost in two of those appearances, including each of the last two years.

Shelton is one of six Americans who were seeded in the 2026 U.S. Open draw, joining Learner Tien (No. 14), Taylor Fritz (No. 9), Frances Tiafoe (No. 11), Brandon Nakashima (No. 16), Tommy Paul (No. 20).

For Hurkacz, it is another early exit from the final tennis major of the year. He has competed in eight U.S. Opens now, but is still looking for his first trip to the third round.

In his career, his best major finish came at Wimbledon in 2021, when he reached the semifinals before losing to Matteo Berrettini in four sets.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Katie Boulter blown away by Karolina Muchova
articles.summary: British No 1 broken in every service game and bageled in second set as US Open campaign unravels at hands of Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova in under an hour; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The British No 1 was broken in all seven of her service games in a chastening 6-1 6-0 defeat inside 58 minutes on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

Boulter traded breaks with Muchova at the start of the first set only for the 2026 Wimbledon finalist to pull clear and put on a clinic for her beleaguered opponent.

Boulter double faulted eight times and produced 22 unforced errors in a nightmare, error-strewn performance that left her hopes of progressing in tatters.

"It was a tough day at the office for Boulter, and that is where Muchova deserves so much credit. She is such an all-round player. The focus was definitely on Muchova rather than what Boulter didn't do.

"The highlight reel from the match was outstanding. There were so many incredible shots and great rallies. She's got the variation, using the little short chip cross-court, following the ball in and knocking off volleys at the net. She can do anything.

"She has reached the French Open and Wimbledon finals and is great on hard courts. If she can stay healthy, she has the experience, mentality, confidence and belief to win one of these tournaments one day."

"You've got to focus on the positives, and that was how well Muchova played.

"She showed us every trick in the book. She has so much in her repertoire. She's playing with a lot of confidence for something who hasn't played a lot since Wimbledon.

"Not a good day at the office for Boulter."

"Karolina Muchova has yet to win a Grand Slam in her career but played some exceptional tennis. On that evidence, she has brilliant potential in this tournament.

"A day to forget for Katie Boulter. She just wasn't there and lost her serve seven times out of seven. That does not give you a chance."

Choinski four-day first-round run brought to end

Britain's Jan Choinski made it to day four at the US Open, but was still a first-round casualty.

The towering German-born 30-year-old was beaten in straight sets by fellow beanpole, Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp.

Getting to the first Wednesday at Flushing Meadows is usually a notable achievement for a British player.

But Choinski's stay at the tournament was only extended after his first-round match was pushed back by the rain in New York.

A handful of players were already through to round three by the time Choinski took to the court, but he was soundly beaten in the big-serving battle 6-3 6-1 7-6 (5) in just under two hours.

Choinski is coached by his girlfriend Sophia, who was shouting encouragement from his players' box.

He said: "She always tries to help me, tries to keep me positive, for sure.

"In the first set it was quite good, I had some chances but from that point it got tough.

"The guy was playing aggressively and she just keeps me fighting and motivated. But in a match like that it's quite tough."
